newsitem.title: ISRAEL: European diplomacy falls short in Mideast crisis.
newsitem.headline: European diplomacy falls short in Mideast crisis.

text.p: If Washington's envoy stumbles during his crisis mission to salvage crumbling Israeli-PLO peace moves, the door may open for the European Union to capitalise on its regional ambitions.
But as the West Bank seethes with unrest and Israeli bulldozers rip into a hillside in Arab East Jerusalem for a new Jewish settlement, Europe so far has failed to mount a credible diplomatic thrust.

A trio of European Middle East tours in March -- by top-level French, German and EU diplomats -- were long on good intentions but short on results to defuse the crisis between Israel and the PLO or to revive Syrian-Israeli peace talks.

Most hopes for replacing Israeli-Palestinian clashes with dialogue now rest on the shoulders of veteren U.S. envoy Dennis Ross, due in the region on Thursday. The White House has said Ross would consult both Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Israel says European censure of Jewish settlement plans has hardened its belief it cannot trust the EU as an honest broker.
Miguel Angel Moratinos, Europe's Middle East envoy, is nonetheless optimistic the 15-member EU can parlay its clout as chief financier of Israel-PLO peace deals into diplomatic might.

"We supply 53 percent of total international aid to the Palestinians," Moratinos told Reuters. "We have to convert this understanding about the economic role of the European Union and put it in a much more political framework."
But EU efforts are handicapped by squabbles among member states over how much political muscle they need to flex to nudge Israel and its Arab neighbours towards a final peace.
France has been most outspoken on the need to carve out deeper regional influence.

"France has acted quite passively," French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said while on his tour to Israel, Syria and Lebanon earlier this month. "It was not a normal situation. We decided that things could not continue like that because we have interests."
But German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel warned European diplomats not to bite off more than they could chew.
"I've tried to warn against overstating our capacity," Kinkel told Israeli academics in Jerusalem in March.
Moratinos, a Spaniard appointed Europe's first special envoy last October, says his post has brought focus to EU moves.
"My idea is to come from what has been perceived as European cacophony with what I can qualify as a European symphony."
"Both de Charette and Kinkel asked me to brief them before they started their trips to the Middle East so it proves that the mechanism is working perfectly," Moratinos said.
But Europe has not translated better coordination among member states into breakthroughs.
De Charette gambled French diplomatic capital in a bid to try to revive long-stalled talks between Damascus and arch-foe Israel -- a task that has eluded US diplomats.

Asked what France, welcomed by Arabs as a foil to Israel's key U.S. ally, could bring as a mediator that the United States could not, de Charette bristled: "We are not in competition with the United States. Maybe we will be complementary."

But unable to budge Syria and Israel from their rigid conditions to open talks on the fate of the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, de Charette downgraded his shuttle to an "opportunity to understand the situation."
Moratinos has not fared much better.
A greater obstacle to European efforts is Israel's deep aversion to accepting a mediator other than its U.S. ally.
"If they want to mediate they have to enjoy trust and confidence equally on both sides," Israeli foreign ministry spokesman Ygal Palmor told Reuters.
Palmor said Europe's support of United Nations resolutions criticising Israeli moves in Jerusalem were "useless".

"Taking sides by pushing U.N. resolutions which have pure declarative value and no practical value...was a totally useless step which only helps to escalate tensions," he said. "It leaves a big question mark concerning their possibilities."

One EU official in Tel Aviv said that while Arabs contended Washington was skewed towards Israel, the United States, which gives Israel $3 billion annually in aid, had the brute strength to carry them into peace talks. "Europe can't drag Israel along," the official said.
